baseline_fp32_measurements.note: 7.3x latency increase for 1.3x model size = thrashing regime
OOM killer fired during model load; memory monitor captured the collapse

splitinfer_streaming_partitioner.note: Streaming solver assigns all layers to FPGA; peak FPGA DDR2 footprint is the largest single layer (100 MB), regardless of total model size. Baseline at this size would thrash (6+ GB RSS); at 9 GB baseline OOM-kills.

capacity_unlock_summary.finding: SplitInfer's streaming partitioner handles models that are ~60x larger than their per-layer peak resident footprint. Dense MLPs up to 9.4 GB cannot run on Jetson Orin Nano alone (OOM killed), while SplitInfer can in principle stream arbitrary-depth models through 128 MB FPGA DDR2.
caveats: SplitInfer's actual measured latency on a 5.5 GB model was not recorded — the 180-layer runtime call timed out at 120s, and debugging the full end-to-end path was deferred. The 463.7 ms figure is the partitioner's analytical estimate.
The actual hardware per-layer cost (~5 ms USB round-trip) means measured SplitInfer latency would be ~900 ms minimum for 180 layers, ~2x the analytical estimate.

The partitioner's streaming cost model does not yet price in per-layer weight download (transfer_to_fpga) over USB; for FP32 weights at 40 MB/s the 100 MB peak layer alone takes 2.5 seconds per layer to download, making the honest end-to-end latency ~7.5 minutes for 180 layers. This is the architectural limit — SplitInfer wins on capacity, not latency.
